items.prompt: A singly linked list must be scanned once, using O(1) extra space, to return a middle node. Which state best matches the requirement?
constraints: The list is singly linked and acyclic for this task.
Only O(1) auxiliary references are permitted.

options.text: Advance slow by one next link and fast by two next links per valid iteration.
Binary-search the list by repeatedly jumping to midpoint indices.
Store every node in an array and return the node at index floor(n/2).
Move a pointer only when consecutive payload values differ.

feedback.reason: A 1:2 speed ratio lets slow reach a middle boundary when fast reaches the end, using only two references.

blocks.text: Both pointers follow the same next relation, but fast covers twice as many edges. When fast exhausts the list, slow has covered approximately half the path. An array also finds a middle but uses O(n) extra space; binary search assumes random access; value changes are unrelated to structural distance. The exact even-length convention depends on initialization and loop guard.

blocks.title: Relative-speed signal
blocks.text: Use fixed-speed pointers when repeated application of one successor relation encodes the desired relative position.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.array_then_index: This violates the O(1)-extra-space requirement by storing all node references.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search_nodes: A singly linked list cannot jump directly to midpoint indices without additional indexing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.compare_values: Payload equality does not measure how far a pointer has traversed.

items.prompt: slow and fast start at the same head. Each completed loop advances slow once and fast twice. Ignoring termination for the moment, which relation holds after t completed loops?
constraints: Each stated iteration completes both advances.
Distance is measured in traversed next edges.

options.text: Their distances depend on the payload values encountered.
slow has traversed 2t edges and fast has traversed t edges.
slow has traversed t edges and fast has traversed 2t edges.
Both have traversed t edges because they started together.

feedback.reason: The loop's defining invariant is the fixed 1:2 edge-advance ratio.

blocks.text: Starting together sets both initial distances to zero. Every completed iteration adds one edge to slow's distance and two to fast's, so the distances are t and 2t. This relation explains middle finding and relative phase in cycles. Different start nodes or step sizes add an offset, and invalid end dereferences must still be prevented by the guard.

blocks.title: Distance invariant
blocks.text: After t complete 1:2 updates from a shared start, slow has crossed t edges and fast has crossed 2t.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_distance: Equal starts do not cancel the different per-iteration step counts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.2t_and_t: This reverses the declared speeds of the two pointers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.depends_on_values: Traversal distance is determined by links and step counts, not payload values.

items.prompt: For A -> B -> C -> D, the contract requires the first middle B. slow starts at A and advances one step whenever fast can advance two. Which initialization gives the required phase under the guard fast != null and fast.next != null?
constraints: The list length may be even.
The required even-length result is the first middle.

options.text: Initialize fast at whichever central payload is smaller.
Initialize fast = tail, so slow never moves.
Initialize fast = head, so slow stops at C.
Initialize fast = head.next, so slow stops at B.

feedback.reason: Starting fast one node ahead shifts the phase so slow selects the first middle for an even-length list.

blocks.text: With fast at B, the first loop moves slow to B and fast to D; the next guard fails because D.next is null, so B is returned. With both at A, two valid loops place slow at C, the second middle. Both conventions can be correct under different contracts. The required result must be stated before choosing initialization.

blocks.title: Phase rule
blocks.text: For even lengths, derive initialization and guard from the required first- or second-middle convention.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fast_at_a: This phase returns the second middle C under the stated guard.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fast_at_d: Starting at the tail does not maintain the intended half-progress relation from the list entry.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.choose_by_values: Middle position is structural and independent of payload ordering.

items.prompt: A middle-finding routine that previously started slow = head and fast = head is changed to start both at a new dummy whose next is head, while keeping the same guard and returning slow. What must be checked?
constraints: The loop guard and return expression are otherwise unchanged.
dummy is not part of the desired logical output.

options.text: The extra starting node changes the phase and may return dummy or a different middle unless the contract is adjusted.
A dummy can never affect any pointer result because it is not a data node.
Every data-node payload is implicitly shifted by one.
The dummy enables direct access to the middle index.

feedback.reason: Relative-speed algorithms depend on start offsets; traversing an extra sentinel changes those offsets even when the sentinel is not logical output.

blocks.text: A sentinel does not alter the data-node chain, but it adds one edge to the traversal path from the chosen start. The slow/fast phase and termination position therefore need to be rederived. The routine might intentionally use a dummy to obtain a predecessor or first-middle convention, but that is a deliberate contract choice, not an automatic equivalence.

blocks.title: Offset rule
blocks.text: An implementation-only predecessor still changes pointer phase when the algorithm traverses through it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.answer_never_changes: Logical membership and algorithmic phase are different; an implementation-only node can still affect traversal offsets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_shift: Adding a predecessor changes traversal distance from the start but does not mutate any data-node payload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_access_enabled: A sentinel provides one fixed predecessor, not indexed access to arbitrary positions.

items.prompt: slow advances one link and fast advances two until fast reaches the end of an n-node acyclic list. No index or stored node array exists. What are the time and extra-space costs?
constraints: The input is a standard singly linked list.
The algorithm does not modify the list.

feedback.reason: Fast traverses the list's length in a constant fraction of n iterations, and only two pointer references are maintained.

blocks.text: The loop performs roughly n/2 iterations, but asymptotically that is O(n); each iteration does constant work. The method does not access position n/2 directly. slow and fast, plus fixed local state, use O(1) extra space. Building an array of node references would permit indexed lookup afterward but would cost O(n) preprocessing time and O(n) space.

blocks.title: Cost rule
blocks.text: About n/2 constant-work iterations remain O(n), while a fixed number of references remains O(1) extra space.

items.prompt: slow references node X(value=5) and fast references a distinct node Y(value=5). Under a fast/slow traversal, has a pointer meeting occurred?
constraints: X and Y are separately allocated nodes.
Duplicate values are allowed in the list.

options.text: It cannot be decided without numeric node indices.
No. Equal payloads do not count; X and Y must be the same node object.
Yes. All nodes in one list have the same node type.
Yes. Equal values are sufficient for convergence.

feedback.reason: Pointer convergence is an identity event, and X and Y are explicitly distinct objects.

blocks.text: Fast and slow may visit many nodes with equal payloads, especially in lists with duplicates. Treating equal values as a meeting can terminate early at unrelated positions. Reference equality directly answers whether both variables designate one structural node; numeric indices are neither intrinsic nor required.

blocks.title: Meeting rule
blocks.text: Pointer convergence means reference identity, never merely equal payloads or node types.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_equal_values: Payload equality can occur at different positions and does not establish a pointer meeting.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_same_type: Sharing a node class or representation says nothing about object identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unknown_without_indices: Reference equality decides the meeting without random-access indices.

items.prompt: One loop iteration should advance slow once and fast twice in an ordinary acyclic list. Order the checks and updates so no invalid next dereference occurs.
constraints: The language evaluates fast.next.next by dereferencing fast and then fast.next.
The list may have even or odd length.

elements.text: Using the validated pre-update state, set slow = slow.next and fast = fast.next.next.

feedback.reason: Both objects needed by the two-link expression must be validated before the fast update is evaluated.

items: Confirm `fast != null` before evaluating any field through fast.
Using that validated pre-update state, advance slow once and fast twice.

blocks.text: The two pointer assignments have no required order after both guards when each right-hand side uses the pre-update state; combining them removes the previous false ordering dependency. Short-circuit `fast != null && fast.next != null` expresses the same guard order.

items.prompt: Select all scenarios where the standard fast/slow relative-speed invariant is directly applicable without redefining pointer movement.
constraints: Direct applicability means the standard fixed-step proof can be used unchanged.
Both correct cases follow node.next deterministically.

options.text: Finding a middle while both pointers repeatedly follow the same node.next relation.
Moving left or right in a sorted array according to whether a sum is too small or too large.
Detecting convergence while both pointers repeatedly follow the same node.next relation inside a cycle.
Moving window boundaries according to a changing validity predicate.

feedback.reason: Middle and cycle traversals use one deterministic successor relation with a fixed speed ratio; the other scenarios use decision-dependent movement rules.

blocks.text: The fast/slow proof tracks relative distance under repeated application of node.next. Sorted pair search and variable windows also use two positions, but their movement is selected from data or validity conditions rather than a fixed 1:2 successor application. Those techniques need different invariants. The presence of two pointers alone is not the transfer signal.

blocks.title: Transfer rule
blocks.text: Reuse the standard proof only when both pointers repeatedly follow the same deterministic successor with fixed step counts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_pair_sum: Its pointer moves are chosen by an ordering comparison, not by a fixed relative speed along one successor function.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_window: Window endpoints advance according to validity maintenance, not a constant speed ratio.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.middle_next_chain: This is a canonical case where end progress encodes half progress.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.cycle_next_chain: This is a canonical case where relative phase changes by one per iteration inside the cycle.

items.prompt: For an even-length list, why must the middle-finding contract specify first versus second middle before choosing initial pointer phases?

options.text: Different slow/fast initializations and guards land on different middle nodes, so the phase is part of the output contract.
All fast/slow variants return the same node for an even list.
The smaller payload determines which middle is correct.
Only fast's final position matters; slow initialization cannot affect the result.

feedback.reason: Relative speed locates a midpoint interval, and initialization/loop guard select which representative the contract returns.

blocks.text: Starting slow=head versus slow=dummy or changing whether fast advances before the loop can produce first or second middle. Payload values do not define the midpoint; node position and pointer phase do.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_middle_always: Even lists have two central nodes and pointer phase distinguishes them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_choose_middle: Middle is a structural position, independent of node values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fast_only: Slow's phase determines which node it references when the guard stops.

items.prompt: A fast/slow routine uses reference equality to detect convergence. Why is comparing node values insufficient?

options.text: Distinct nodes may carry equal values, so value equality can report a false meeting; convergence means the same node object.
Linked-list values are guaranteed unique by the structure.
Pointers cannot be compared, so value equality is the only possible test.
Only fast's payload matters because slow controls traversal.

feedback.reason: Cycle convergence is an identity relation on nodes, not an equality relation on payloads.

blocks.text: Two independently allocated nodes can both store 5 while occupying different positions and next links. A cycle detector must compare references; otherwise repeated values in an acyclic list can be misclassified as a cycle.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reference_not_comparable: Reference equality is exactly the structural operation needed for pointer convergence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fast_value_only: Both pointer identities determine whether they occupy the same node.

items.prompt: For a list with an even number of nodes, what determines whether fast/slow returns the first or second middle node?
constraints: Slow advances one node per iteration.
Fast's initial position and loop guard are configurable.

options.text: The initialization phase and whether the loop checks fast or fast.next determine which middle convention is reached.
options.explanation: A one-step phase shift changes the stopping node on even length.

options.text: The larger middle payload is always selected.
options.explanation: Middle selection is structural, not value-based.

options.text: Fast moving at twice the speed always returns the same middle under every guard.
options.explanation: Initialization and guard affect the stopping condition.

options.text: Sorting the list first makes the middle convention deterministic.
options.explanation: Sorting changes values and is irrelevant to positional convention.

feedback.reason: Fast/slow is a family of position conventions; the initial phase and stopping guard are part of the algorithm contract.

blocks.text: For even-length lists, one loop may stop when fast is null and another when fast.next is null, yielding adjacent middle nodes. The choice must be stated and tested rather than inferred from the speed ratio alone.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.payload_order: Middle selection is structural, not value-based.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fast_speed_only: Initialization and guard affect the stopping condition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.list_sorting: Sorting changes values and is irrelevant to positional convention.

items.prompt: Why does a two-to-one speed ratio allow cycle detection but not directly identify the cycle entry?
constraints: The list may contain a cycle.
A meeting point can occur away from the entry.

options.text: The first phase establishes convergence; a second equal-speed phase is needed to use the entry-distance relation.
options.explanation: Meeting and entry location are distinct claims.

options.text: The faster pointer always reaches the entry first, so the first meeting is the entry.
options.explanation: The first meeting can be anywhere inside the cycle.

options.text: The entry is the first node whose value matches slow's value.
options.explanation: Payload values do not encode cycle position.

options.text: Restart fast at head but keep slow at the meeting point and preserve the two-to-one ratio.
options.explanation: The entry phase requires equal one-link movement.

feedback.reason: Relative speed proves repeated-node convergence, while entry recovery needs a separate distance argument.

blocks.text: The meeting node depends on the cycle length and phase. Resetting one pointer and moving both at one link per step aligns the distance from head to entry with the distance from the meeting point around the cycle.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.speed_is_entry: The first meeting can be anywhere inside the cycle.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.value_match: Payload values do not encode cycle position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.restart_fast_only: The entry phase requires equal one-link movement.

items.prompt: Before a loop advances fast by two links, which evaluation order is safe on a possibly acyclic list?
constraints: Fast may be null.
Fast.next may be null.

options.text: Check fast and fast.next for null before evaluating either dereference in the two-link advance.
options.explanation: Short-circuit guards prevent invalid pointer access.

options.text: Advance fast first and inspect nullability afterward.
options.explanation: The invalid dereference occurs before the check.

options.text: Check slow because fast is always ahead of a valid slow pointer.
options.explanation: Fast can reach the end independently.

options.text: Check the node value for null instead of checking pointer references.
options.explanation: A payload can be any legal value and does not guard a pointer.

feedback.reason: Pointer guards must precede the dereferences they protect.

blocks.text: In an acyclic list, fast can be null or can point to a final node. Checking fast and fast.next first makes the two-link move safe; a value check or slow-only guard does not.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.advance_then_check: The invalid dereference occurs before the check.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.slow_guard_only: Fast can reach the end independently.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.payload_guard: A payload can be any legal value and does not guard a pointer.

items.prompt: A problem exposes a function `next(x)` rather than explicit list nodes. Which linked-list pattern transfers directly?
constraints: The function is deterministic.
The goal is to detect whether a state repeats.

options.text: Use slow=f(next(slow)) and fast=f(f(fast)) with state identity or equality defined by the problem.
options.explanation: A deterministic successor function has the same functional-graph convergence structure.

options.text: Use opposite array ends because every successor function is ordered.
options.explanation: A successor function does not provide an ordered array boundary.

options.text: Sort generated states before testing repetition.
options.explanation: Sorting can destroy transition order and does not detect functional cycles.

options.text: Count only numeric values without defining state equality.
options.explanation: The transfer requires a well-defined state identity relation.

feedback.reason: Fast/slow transfers to deterministic successor systems when state equality and successor application are explicit.

blocks.text: A linked list is a special case of a functional graph. The same relative-speed convergence applies, but the implementation must define whether states are references, immutable values, or another identity suitable for equality.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.array_two_ends: A successor function does not provide an ordered array boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_states: Sorting can destroy transition order and does not detect functional cycles.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.payload_frequency: The transfer requires a well-defined state identity relation.
